text:
With ≤16 users/category, binary HR@10 is coarse: one hit changes a category’s rate by ≥6.25 percentage points. Percentile bootstrap intervals can have poor coverage and collapse when every observed outcome is identical; more resamples cannot fix this information shortage. Report hits/sample size and a binomial interval per category—Wilson as an approximate option, Clopper–Pearson when conservative coverage is required under independent binomial sampling. Bootstrap coverage failures are established in [Wang (2013)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167715213002940). For model comparisons, retain user pairing and report discordant counts; methods for paired binary proportions are reviewed by [Fagerland et al.](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.6148).

Recommended application: compute each user’s paired hit difference, resample users within each category while preserving model pairs, then average the four category differences with equal weights. Label any percentile interval exploratory at this sample size; identical observed differences can produce misleadingly narrow intervals. User resampling with fixed candidates addresses user variation conditional on that candidate realization. Repeated candidate draws with fixed users address candidate-draw variability; use the same draw for both models and report this variability separately, without treating repeated draws as additional users. With a pinned evaluator seed, candidate variability remains unmeasured. These distinctions matter because sampled ranking metrics can even reverse model ordering in expectation and do not estimate full-catalog metrics faithfully ([Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). Any population interpretation also requires representative user selection; bootstrap intervals cannot correct selection bias.
